title: Research
practiceStatement: I study how bodies, sound and dress make culture, then translate it for people who build things.

projects.name: Sonic Anti-Intimacy
projects.oneLineOutcome: Sound designed as a cocoon, not a cage.

slides.text: What, in sonic terms, might characterise the opposite of intimacy?
Four places where sound is present but does not connect: headphones, shopping-mall Muzak, voice assistants, Cage's 4'33".

image.alt: Four objects: headphones, a shopping-mall speaker, a smart speaker, the score of 4'33"
image.brief: Four objects or screenshots in a grid

slides.notes: Where I listened. This project has no fieldwork, so this slide shows the evidence.

bullets: Muzak scores music on tempo, rhythm, instrumentation and orchestra size: the Stimulus Quotient
With music playing, customers stayed about three minutes longer (MacLeod, 1979)

image.alt: Diagram of the Muzak Stimulus Quotient: tempo, rhythm, instrumentation, orchestra size
image.brief: Redrawn diagram of the Stimulus Quotient

slides.notes: Observation. Proof object: the Stimulus Quotient, redrawn. Source: MacLeod, 1979.

slides.text: Sonic anti-intimacy is presence without connection: the active engineering of disconnection through sound.
slides.notes: Interpretation. From the conclusion of the essay.

slides.text: Streaming mood playlists are the new Muzak. Sound is a design decision, with consequences for how people treat each other in a room.

image.alt: Streaming mood playlists beside a Muzak advertisement
image.brief: Spotify mood playlist screenshots beside a Muzak ad

slides.notes: Implication. Anderson, Neo-Muzak, 2015. Check the journal citation before quoting.

projects.name: Tokyo Drift
projects.subtitle: Fashion, sound, movement. The graffiti of the soul.
projects.context: University of Oxford, 2025. Fieldwork in Shibuya and Shimokitazawa, August to September 2024
projects.oneLineOutcome: To understand a cultural space, be a body within the crowd.
projects.consentNote: Confirm each named participant agreed to be named in a public portfolio, not only in the thesis.

slides.text: How did a musical culture rooted in African American struggle dig itself into Tokyo's nightlife, and what does the body do with borrowed style?
slides.notes: Question. Prologue and epilogue of the thesis.

slides.text: Three weeks. Eight clubs. Seven interviews and twelve informal conversations with DJs, rappers, designers and club owners.

image.alt: Map of Shibuya and Shimokitazawa with the fieldwork route, beside fieldnote pages
image.brief: Map of the two districts with the route, and fieldnote pages

slides.notes: Fieldwork. Seven interviews: four formal, two semi-structured, one by email (thesis Appendix B).

slides.text: At HVEN the entrance is hidden and the rooms are joined by glass, so you can watch without being obvious.
bullets: Dabo's debut cover outfit was chosen by his label, Def Jam Japan
Coma-Chi set personal Japanese lyrics over an American beat
YESBØWY took his dark green nails from a DJ he once saw in white gloves

image.alt: Annotated plan of HVEN showing the three rooms and the glass walls
image.brief: TO MAKE: redrawn HVEN plan, annotated

slides.notes: Observation. Proof object: Zai's own redrawn, annotated plan of HVEN (the Void, the Hanger, the Deck). The plan in the thesis comes from the club's website, so redraw it.

slides.text: The club is a wall that is rewritten every night. Every outfit is a tag and every beat is a mark. Borrowed paint on local walls is authorship, not imitation.
slides.notes: Interpretation. Graffiti as ornament (Schacter, 2016). Image-led, one line.

slides.text: Style is made by recombining borrowed codes. HVEN shows how to design connection when there is no leader to follow.

image.alt: A look worn by a performer beside the glass wall at HVEN
image.brief: A look from Dabo or YESBØWY beside the HVEN glass wall, with permission

slides.text: To truly understand a cultural space, it is necessary to be a body within the crowd.

projects.name: Tagging the Body
projects.subtitle: Sound, Fabric and Affect in London Clubs
projects.context: MA Cultural and Creative Industries, King's College London, 2026
projects.oneLineOutcome: The concept now works as a tool for designing venues, brands and garments.
projects.consentNote: Use first names or pseudonyms. Keep Kit's comments about dressing in less accepting venues out unless he agrees.

slides.text: How do sound and fabric produce the body as an affective and inscribed surface in London clubs?
Sensory ethnography and autoethnography. Five participants, four transcribed interviews and a structured fieldwork log.

image.alt: A redacted page of the fieldwork log beside an annotated transcript
image.brief: Redacted log page or annotated transcript

slides.notes: Fieldwork. Three solo interviews and one joint interview.

slides.text: Asked what a good club feels like, every participant said: safety.
slides.quote: It reduces all the anxiety that you might have felt about what you're wearing, about the space you're in. (Tallulah, on the bass)
slides.notes: Observation. Longest and most visual slide of the project. Then the meaning split: safe people, or being enveloped by sound.

slides.text: Archival capital: the value produced when repeated, chosen, sensory encounter leaves traces on the body.

image.alt: Diagram of the four stages of archival capital
image.brief: Four stages: accumulation, expression, legibility, conversion, failure or refusal

slides.notes: Interpretation. Proof object: the four stages as a designed diagram, with failure given equal weight.

slides.text: A room has to feel safe before a body will surrender to it. Venues, brands and garments can design for the conditions that let people accumulate and show what they carry.

image.alt: A venue beside a garment detail
image.brief: A venue and a garment detail side by side

slides.text: The concept now works as a tool for designing venues, brands and garments.
